strengths: Very extensive empirical benchmark: 15 LLMs across families/sizes/openness, 3 large survey datasets (WGM, OQA, WVS) spanning diverse topics and demographics, 3 distribution elicitation methods (verbalized, self-random, paraphrase), plus a smaller logit-based study — this breadth is a genuine asset for the community and provides a useful reference benchmark.

The paper moves beyond majority-vote evaluation common in prior SD-prompting work to a fully distributional framing, which is a more faithful and pluralistically-aligned way to assess whether LLMs capture intra-group disagreement.

Multiple well-motivated research questions (RQ1-RQ5) are addressed with corresponding experiments, including sample-efficiency of calibration (as few as 5 examples), per-demographic breakdowns, out-of-domain generalization of the regression calibrator, and effects of post-training stages (SFT/DPO/RLVR) on alignment — this systematic coverage yields several practically useful findings for practitioners.

Reasonably transparent reporting: full per-model tables in the appendix, prompt templates provided for reproducibility, explicit limitations and ethics discussion, and an honest acknowledgment that calibration effects vary across demographic subgroups rather than uniformly improving alignment.

The finding that calibration substantially reduces variance across models/datasets/elicitation methods (making elicitation-method or model choice less critical after calibration) is a useful, actionable takeaway.
weaknesses: The central comparison between 'SD prompting' (zero-shot) and 'calibration' (trained with substantial in-domain supervision, up to 80% of ground-truth distributions) is somewhat asymmetric: because the regression is fit directly against held-out true response distributions from the same dataset/demographic structure, it is close to expected that it will reduce systematic bias and improve the alignment metric. The paper would benefit from clearer framing of this as a bias-correction exercise rather than implying a novel scientific finding that supervision categorically 'beats' prompting.

The statistical testing methodology behind the bolded significant differences in the main results table (Table 1, aggregated over many questions) is not clearly specified (test used, sample sizes, multiple-comparison correction), which limits reproducibility of the significance claims; only Section 5.1 explicitly describes a paired t-test with Bonferroni correction for the granular demographic analysis, and there it explicitly notes most differences are not significant due to small per-demographic sample sizes (4-6 examples), which undercuts confidence in several RQ3/RQ6 claims.

The regression calibrator itself is technically minimal (independent per-answer-choice regression with post-hoc normalization, optimized for MSE rather than the evaluation metric), and the paper's exploration of alternative constrained formulations is only briefly mentioned; this limits the technical/methodological contribution beyond the empirical benchmarking exercise.

Ground-truth 'human response distributions' for fine-grained SD subgroups are derived from relative frequencies within survey samples, but subgroup sample sizes (especially for granular demographics) are not reported/discussed, raising concern about the reliability of the reference distributions themselves, which propagates into both evaluation and calibration training.

Some methodological choices are inconsistently applied without full justification (e.g., different sampling budgets n=3 vs n=5 across elicitation methods, decisions made based on 'we found little variance' without supporting numbers), and the practical guidance in the discussion, while sensible, is fairly qualitative/hedged rather than derived from rigorous statistical comparison.

strengths: Broad, well-designed empirical study spanning three diverse survey datasets (WGM, OQA, WVS), 15 LLMs of varying openness/size/post-training, and three distribution elicitation methods (verbalized, self-random, paraphrase), which is considerably more comprehensive than prior single-method, single-dataset studies of sociodemographic (SD) prompting.

Correctly reframes the evaluation problem from majority-vote/single-answer matching (a known flaw in prior SD-prompting literature) to full distributional alignment using an ordinal-aware metric (1 - Wasserstein distance), which is methodologically more appropriate for Likert-type survey data.

The proposed supervised calibration approach is simple, cheap, and practically useful: it consistently improves alignment (94.8% of settings, ~16.3% average), reduces variance across models/datasets/methods, and works with as few as 5 labeled examples, offering directly actionable guidance to practitioners.

Goes beyond aggregate results to examine per-demographic-group effects (RQ3), effects of reduced supervision (RQ4), out-of-domain generalization of the regression calibrator (Section 6.3), and interactions with post-training stages (SFT/DPO/RLVR, RQ5), giving a multi-faceted picture rather than a single headline number.

Thoughtful discussion section that explicitly engages with the ethical/conceptual risk of essentializing sociodemographic identities and situates the contribution relative to pluralistic alignment goals, along with a reasonably candid limitations section.
Reasonable reproducibility support: prompts for all elicitation/demographic conditions are given in appendix tables, and dataset/demographic details are specified.
weaknesses: The central calibration claim lacks a crucial baseline: since regression is trained per dataset-LLM-elicitation setting on held-out questions from the same distribution, and calibration is shown to strongly shrink variance (both within and across settings, up to ~3-5x), it is unclear how much of the reported improvement reflects genuine correction of demographic-specific LLM biases versus a trivial 'regression toward the mean/typical human distribution shape' effect that would occur even with weak or uninformative LLM inputs. A baseline that predicts a constant/average human distribution (ignoring the LLM output) is needed to disentangle this.

Many individual sociodemographic-level findings (RQ3) are not statistically significant due to very small per-group sample sizes (4-6 examples), which weakens confidence in claims about which specific demographics benefit or are harmed by calibration, and about which LLMs are 'better aligned' with which groups.

The regression calibrator must be retrained per dataset-LLM-elicitation-method combination, which somewhat limits the claimed 'simplicity and generality' of the approach in practice, despite the encouraging few-shot (5-example) and cross-dataset generalization results.

Base results (pre-calibration) show that SD prompting provides inconsistent, often negligible benefit over demographic-agnostic prompting, which is a useful negative finding but also means much of the paper's positive signal is carried entirely by the supervised calibration step rather than by improved elicitation/prompting itself, somewhat narrowing the paper's novelty relative to prior calibration/confidence-elicitation literature applied in a new context.

The subsetting of questions (2 per category for OQA/WVS) and reliance on only the 'most powerful' model per family in the main text could limit the robustness/generalizability of the dataset- and model-level conclusions, since results are demonstrably dataset- and model-dependent throughout.

Presentation is heavily table-driven with dense numeric reporting; the text sometimes restates table numbers without deeper synthesis or interpretation of why certain patterns emerge (e.g., why OLMo aligns best with WVS specifically), leaving some explanations speculative (e.g., the discussion of income and post-training effects).

strengths: Large-scale, systematic empirical study spanning 15 LLMs (varying openness, size, post-training), 3 diverse survey datasets, and 3 broadly-applicable distribution elicitation methods (verbalized, self-random, paraphrase), yielding a comprehensive benchmark rather than a narrow single-setting result.

Addresses a genuine gap in prior literature: most prior SD-prompting evaluations collapse to majority-vote answers; this work evaluates full response distributions, which is a more faithful test of pluralistic alignment.

The central empirical claim (simple supervised calibration improves and stabilizes distributional alignment) is supported with appropriate statistical testing (paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction), consistent effect sizes across the vast majority of settings (94.8%), and a clear variance-reduction analysis (Fig. 2) that strengthens the interpretive story about LLMs exaggerating group differences.

Includes thoughtful control experiments that anticipate obvious objections: comparison with few-shot prompting (to check the regression is doing more than mere example exposure), an out-of-domain/cross-dataset generalization test (Appendix A.4), a minimal-data-efficiency study (RQ4), and a small logit-based elicitation comparison, all of which bolster robustness of the main claim.

Reasonably detailed reproducibility materials: full prompt templates, dataset/demographic descriptions, and stated intent to open-source, which supports a Findings-level (and arguably higher) standard of reproducibility.
Thoughtful discussion of ethical risks (essentializing sociodemographic identity, adversarial misuse) and appropriate caution about overclaiming what calibration achieves for individual groups.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (per-answer-choice supervised regression to rescale LLM distributions toward human distributions, using in-domain held-out examples) is conceptually simple, essentially a calibration/rescaling procedure; the novelty is more in the scale/framing of the evaluation than in method design, and this should temper claims of contribution beyond "benchmark" value.

Because the regression is trained on other questions from the same dataset (same answer-choice format and scale biases), part of the alignment gain likely reflects correction of a fixed, dataset-specific answer-scale bias rather than genuine improvement in modeling group-specific opinion structure; while the out-of-domain generalization experiment partially mitigates this concern, the paper does not fully disentangle "scale recalibration" from "demographic alignment."

The individual sociodemographic-group analysis (RQ3, Section 5) is based on very small per-group sample sizes (4-6 examples), yields mostly non-significant differences, yet is used to support qualitative narrative claims (e.g., disparate calibration benefits for historically marginalized vs. advantaged subgroups) that are not strongly statistically substantiated.
The post-training analysis (RQ5) is conducted on a single model family (OLMo-2), which limits the generalizability of conclusions about how SFT/DPO/RLVR affect distributional alignment.

The "overthinking" explanation for CoT reducing Claude's alignment (Section 4.3) rests on a single qualitative example generalized into a broader claim about larger reasoning models, which is speculative and under-evidenced.

There is a mismatch between the regression's training objective (MSE on split per-choice values) and the evaluation metric (Wasserstein-based opinion alignment), which is acknowledged only briefly as a limitation without deeper analysis of its implications.

The presentation is extremely dense (many large tables, 5 RQs, multiple appendices) which, while thorough, reduces clarity and may make it harder for readers to extract the most decision-relevant findings without extensive cross-referencing.

strengths: Very extensive empirical scope: 3 diverse survey datasets (WGM, OQA, WVS), 15 models spanning openness/size/post-training, 3 distribution elicitation methods (verbalized, self-random, paraphrase), and multiple prompting variants (base, SD, CoT, few-shot), yielding a large and useful benchmark.

Addresses a clear and underexplored gap: prior work on persona/SD prompting mostly evaluates against majority-vote answers rather than full response distributions; this paper's distributional framing is a meaningful methodological improvement and is well motivated.

The central empirical claim (simple supervised calibration substantially and consistently improves distributional alignment, and reduces variance across models/datasets/elicitation methods) is supported by a large number of controlled comparisons with appropriate statistical testing (paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction).

Goes beyond a single headline result with many informative secondary analyses: minimal-data calibration (1-10 examples), comparison against few-shot prompting as a control, per-demographic-group breakdowns, effects of CoT, effects of post-training stages (SFT/DPO/RLVR) on an open model family, and out-of-domain (cross-dataset) generalization of the calibration model.

Good engineering/reproducibility effort: prompts for all elicitation and prompting conditions are given in the appendix, extraction-rate statistics are reported transparently (including model failures/refusals), and the authors commit to open-sourcing code and data.

Thoughtful discussion of limitations and ethical considerations, particularly the risk of essentializing sociodemographic identities and the caution needed when interpreting group-level calibration results.
weaknesses: A key ablation is missing: there is no comparison against a trivial 'regress-to-the-mean' baseline (e.g., simply predicting the average/marginal human response distribution from the training split). Since the calibration regression is fit and evaluated using the same in-domain distribution shapes, it is hard to rule out that much of the reported 16.3% average improvement stems from correcting a few systematic global biases (e.g., overconfidence, extreme answer choices) rather than learning genuinely useful group-conditional information; this materially affects interpretation of the central quantitative claim.

The regression procedure treats each answer-choice position independently and re-normalizes afterward, which is a coarse approach whose sensitivity to answer-choice count/ordering across heterogeneous questions is not fully analyzed; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but does not quantify its impact.

Individual sociodemographic-level analysis (RQ3) is based on very small sample sizes (4-6 examples per group), so most differences are not statistically significant, weakening the evidentiary basis for claims about which specific groups benefit or are harmed by calibration.

The post-training analysis (RQ5) is conducted on a single model family (OLMo-2-7B) with only one model size, limiting generalizability of conclusions about post-training effects on distributional alignment.

The few-shot prompting comparison uses only a single shot count (5-shot) and a small number of runs (3), which is a fairly limited robustness check against the alternative explanation that in-context learning could match calibration with more careful tuning.

The paper is very dense, with heavy reliance on large tables; while thorough, this reduces readability and makes it harder for readers to identify the most decisive findings versus the many secondary results.
